title: What is an 'edge case'?
idea: edge-case enumeration: an edge case is an unusual-but-possible input (empty, zero, just one) that can break a plan that only handles the 'normal' case.

options: An unusual but possible input that might break a simple plan
A mistake in your math
A kind of loop
The last line of a program
exercises.explanation: An edge case is a possible input at the 'edges' of normal — like an empty list or a zero — that a quick plan might miss.

exercises.prompt: Thinking of tricky inputs BEFORE you write code helps you avoid bugs later.
exercises.explanation: Yes. Listing edge cases up front means your plan handles them on purpose, not by accident.

exercises.prompt: You will average a list of scores. Which input is an EDGE case worth thinking about first?
options: An empty list (no scores)
A list of three normal scores
A list of five normal scores
Any list with more than one score
exercises.explanation: An empty list is the tricky one — dividing by zero scores breaks. The 'normal' lists are the easy middle.

exercises.prompt: Why do edge cases deserve special attention?
options: They're easy to forget and often cause the worst bugs
They never actually happen
They make code run faster
They are the normal inputs
exercises.explanation: Edge cases hide at the boundaries. A plan that only handles the middle crashes or lies when a boundary input arrives.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation to its edge-case input.

pairs.right: A list with only one item

exercises.explanation: Each task has a boundary input that stresses it: empty, zero, or a single item. Spotting them is the habit.

exercises.prompt: The 'normal' inputs (a few typical values) are where most bugs hide.
exercises.explanation: No — the normal middle is usually fine. Bugs hide at the edges: empty, zero, one item, the very biggest.

exercises.prompt: Enumerating edge cases is best done...
options: During planning, before writing code
Only after the program crashes
Never — just run it
Only once the code is finished
exercises.explanation: List them while planning. Finding tricky cases before coding is this unit's whole idea.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is NOT an edge case for 'sum a list of numbers'?
options: A list of a few ordinary numbers
An empty list
A list with a single number
A list where every number is zero
exercises.explanation: A few ordinary numbers is the normal case. Empty, single-item, and all-zeros are the edges to check.

exercises.prompt: Order the healthy habit: plan first, then enumerate, then code.
blocks: Write the code to handle all of them
exercises.explanation: Understand, then enumerate edge cases, THEN code. Enumerating early shapes a plan that won't be surprised.

exercises.prompt: The big idea of this lesson:
options: An edge case is an unusual possible input; list them before coding
Edge cases are rare and ignorable
Only normal inputs matter
Edge cases are syntax errors
exercises.explanation: Edge cases are the boundary inputs. Naming them up front is the deepest form of the edge-case habit.
